request.text:
A: So. Mirewood. Did the Court sing for you? Half the Warden songs ended up in those reeds. I can hear my own verses in them.
<long pause>
A: Ysolde offered me a verse for a memory. I said no. I'm told that makes me the only person who's ever refused a bargain in Mirewood.
<long pause>
A: It wasn't the last verse anyway. The fey don't have it either. Whoever kept that one never used the fire.
<long pause>
A: Not here. Ask me again somewhere colder. Some things you only say where your breath shows.
<long pause>
A: But watch the hooded one by the door. They've been a step ahead of you since the ford, and a step ahead of me for twenty years.
<long pause>
A: They don't remember their own names, but they remember the tune. Songs don't burn. I did tell you.
<long pause>
A: There you are. Twenty years I've followed you across this Vale, and you've never once let me catch up.
<long pause>
A: My teacher's teacher kept a Warden songbook from before the Fall. Beside the Song of the Seven, someone drew a face in the margin. That face.
<long pause>
A: Every place a song goes quiet, they've been there first. I thought if I followed long enough, I'd find the verse they were hiding.
<long pause>
A: Can't, or won't?
<long pause>
A: I'm coming with you to the Keep. If anyone hears that verse sung at last, it's going to be me.
<long pause>
A: Pay it back, children, or pay what you've known.
<long pause>
A: Twenty years. And it was sitting in a tower all along, waiting for someone to ask.
<long pause>
A: Whatever you choose up there, every square in the Vale will know what the choice was. I'll make sure of it.
<long pause>
A: Ah, an audience! Stand there and look grave, and I'll sing you something the Wardens wrote before your grandmothers were born.
<long pause>
A: Look at you. Still holding a lute like it owes you money.
<long pause>
A: I left because the songs were moving, and a songkeeper has to move with them. I should have said goodbye. We're terrible at endings. We always think there's another verse.
<long pause>
A: Stay close this time. If the songs are right, the Vale is about to need someone who can tell the whole of it.
<long pause>
A: Seven went over the Greywall high, and seven came home with a fire in the sky. The Wardens kept it and the Wardens sang, and the whole Vale warmed where the hearth-bells rang.
<long pause>
A: That's the Wardens' Song of the Seven. Seven went, seven came home, a gift and a hearth and everyone happy.
<long pause>
A: There's a last verse, too. Nobody has sung it in two hundred years. When a song loses its last verse on purpose, it's usually because the last verse was true.
<long pause>
A: Songs gather where things are about to happen. A starving town, a goblin on a bridge, an ember going cold under the river. This is the best stage in the Vale.
<long pause>
A: And someone I've been following came this way. Never mind who. That's a song for later, somewhere colder.
<long pause>
A: Anything else? I take requests. I don't take criticism.
<long pause>
A: Go on, then. Do something worth a verse.
<long pause>
B: The margin was unkind. I was never that thin.
<long pause>
B: You want the last verse, songkeeper. So do I. Go to the Keep and ask the one who never forgot. I cannot sing it for you.
<long pause>
B: Yes.
